section_summary: The section concludes a report on Japanese press and radio unions, tracing the All Japan News and Radio Workers’ Union’s response to failed strikes, member defections, and disputes over its affiliation with the Congress of Industrial Organizations. It then records a State Department discussion of Japan’s labor situation, a SCAP directive addressing labor shortages on Occupation construction projects, and a despatch enclosing Japanese and English versions of coal miners’ Communist faction meeting minutes.

subfiles.title: Labor Organization in the Press and Radio, concluding chapters, appendix and sources
subfiles.about: Analyzes the organization, policies and labor relations of Japanese newspaper and broadcasting unions through mid-1947.
subfiles.summary: The report describes moderates’ efforts to change AJNRWU leadership and its relationship with the Congress of Industrial Organizations after failed strike calls and the Mainichi union’s departure. It follows the Asahi union’s position and a compromise that preserved AJNRWU membership while allowing local autonomy. A separate account traces the Broadcasting Corporation of Japan’s prolonged personnel and contract dispute. The concluding chapter assesses union structure, wages, job security and management relations; the pages also include the end of an Asahi union contract appendix and a list of interview sources.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Japanese Labor Situation
subfiles.about: Summarizes SCAP labor chief Killan’s assessment of coal output, surplus workers, wages, Communist influence and the future of Japanese unions.
subfiles.summary: Killan attributes the coal shortage to poor equipment, wartime mine deterioration and an inexperienced workforce. He describes SCAP’s opposition to mass layoffs, anticipates pressure to raise wages, identifies Communist influence in several unions, and argues that continued U.S. control is needed to sustain Japanese trade unionism.

subfiles.title: Directive Instructing the Japanese Government to Overcome the Causes of Labor Shortages
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAPIN 1832 and relates Occupation construction labor shortages to ration distribution, transport and delayed contractor payments.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the directive and suggests the cited shortages contribute to wider labor unrest and low production.

subfiles.title: Shortage of Japanese Laborers (SCAPIN 1832)
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through Central Liaison Office
subfiles.about: Orders action to remedy labor shortages on Occupation construction projects, especially Grant Heights.
subfiles.summary: Directs prompt contractor payments, equitable food and clothing rations, transport, and a progress report by December 30.

subfiles.title: Text of a Memorandum Believed to Have Been Prepared by Elements of the Japan Communist Party
subfiles.doc_type: confidential despatch with inserted enclosure identification sheet
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards and interprets an alleged Communist coal miners’ faction memorandum supplied by Vice Minister Esaku Sato.
subfiles.summary: Sebald argues that the enclosed minutes show Communist elements seeking local labor conflict and economic disruption while criticizing Occupation policy. He notes the memorandum’s calls for tax opposition, coal miners’ organizing and union affiliation. Page 287 is an inserted identification sheet for the original enclosure.

subfiles.title: National Fraction of Coal Miners meeting minutes, Japanese original
subfiles.to: Local coal miners’ factions and party leadership
subfiles.about: Records October 4 and October 12, 1947 coal miners’ faction discussions of wages, mine safety, taxes, national coal control and organizing tactics.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese memorandum links local mine struggles to minimum wage demands, tax resistance, safety equipment and national coal control. Its later minutes address divisions among coal miners’ organizations, joint action and possible affiliation with Sambetsu.

subfiles.title: Translation of the National Fraction of Coal Miners memorandum
subfiles.to: Local coal miners’ factions and party leadership
subfiles.about: Translates the opening portion of the coal miners’ faction memorandum and its October 4 meeting minutes.
subfiles.summary: The translation presents the faction’s assessment of international and Japanese economic conditions, then its plan to build workshop and local struggles around minimum wages. It sets out demands concerning tax, allowances and safety equipment, and urges using coal control and production disputes to advance wage campaigns. The translation continues beyond page 303.
